prompt: What rating system best handles teams that rarely play each other?
response_text:
When teams seldom play one another—due to geography, conference alignment, budget, or other reasons—you want a rating system that **makes good inferences across weakly connected networks**, deals well with limited data, and still produces fair comparisons. Here are several strong candidates, their pros/cons, and what “rare matchups” means for choosing one.

---

## What “rarely playing each other” implies

- A **sparse schedule**: many teams never meet directly or have very few shared opponents.
- **Disconnected or weakly connected subgraphs** in the matchup graph.
- Strong dependence on **indirect comparisons** (A beats B, B beats C, so maybe A > C).
- Enormous importance of schedule strength, uncertainty estimates, and carefully combining direct/indirect info.

---

## Rating systems that shine in sparse settings

Here are some of the best options when cross-play is rare:

### 1. Bradley–Terry / Pairwise-Comparison Models

- These are statistical models where every game is viewed as a “paired comparison.” They fit team strengths so that predicted probabilities best match outcomes.  
- They handle indirect information well: the strength of B helps infer matches between A and C, even if they never played.  
- In practice, used in systems with sparse schedules. The “bayesRatings” system for sports is built on Bradley–Terry, combined with Bayesian inference for uncertainty. ([bayesratings.com](https://bayesratings.com/methodology/?utm_source=openai))  
- Pros: Good probabilistic interpretation, naturally handles irregular connections, can incorporate prior beliefs or anchor ratings when data is scarce.  
- Cons: Requires solving a potentially large optimization; combining margin of victory and home/away advantage adds complexity.

### 2. Colley Matrix Method

- Developed by Wesley Colley. Builds a linear system based only on wins/losses, solving for ratings at once rather than iteratively. ([elote.mcginniscommawill.com](https://elote.mcginniscommawill.com/rating_systems/colley.html?utm_source=openai))  
- Rewards strength of schedule implicitly, because beating strong opponents (based on connections through other games) helps more.  
- Key features: order-independence (game order doesn’t matter), bias-free, no margin-of-victory dependence (just outcome). ([elote.mcginniscommawill.com](https://elote.mcginniscommawill.com/rating_systems/colley.html?utm_source=openai))  
- Weaknesses when schedules are completely disconnected: if two groups of teams never play any matches that cross over, there’s no meaningful way to compare them. Also, loses information by ignoring margins of victory. ([metricgate.com](https://metricgate.com/docs/colley-rating-method/?utm_source=openai))

### 3. SRS / KRACH / TrueSkill / Modern Elo Variants

- Many systems use an Elo-style approach: update ratings sequentially after each result. Variants include Glicko (with confidence intervals), TrueSkill, etc.  
- They often incorporate strength of opponent, sometimes margin, and in newer systems they include uncertainty when interactions are rare.  
- Example: “SharpModels” uses dynamic Elo‐style ratings adjusting more from surprise results (beat a strong team) than expected wins. ([sharpmodels.com](https://www.sharpmodels.com/methodology?utm_source=openai))  
- Pros: Fast incremental updates, good online adaptation, uncertainty useful when there are few games.  
- Cons: Early results can be volatile; pure Elo without modification can overrate teams in weak schedules unless you explicitly adjust for strength of schedule or use priors/anchors.

### 4. Hybrid / Multi-Channel Systems

- Systems that combine win-loss information, margins, opponent strength, and additional metrics (like drive efficiency in football) tend to do well.  
- Example: “Saturdaysavant” for college football uses opponent-adjusted scoring, neutralizing home field, and including drive-level data. ([saturdaysavant.com](https://saturdaysavant.com/savant-rating?utm_source=openai))  
- These tend to infer better across indirectly connected teams, since data from many channels helps break ties or fill gaps.

---

## What works *worst*, or what to avoid

- Sole reliance on raw win percentage or total wins without adjusting for opponent strength: easy to inflate ratings via weak schedules.  
- Systems that don’t account for disjoint groups: if teams never play outside their cluster, any “global” ranking is mostly guesswork.  
- Margin-of-victory systems, if used naively, can be manipulated or distorted if weak teams get large blowouts.  

---

## Rule of thumb: best choice depends on how sparse

Here’s a decision guide based on how much cross-play and indirect information you have:

| Scenario | Best rating system | Why it works well |
|---|---|---|
| Very little crossover, mostly intra-group play, few direct comparisons | Bradley–Terry with priors or Pairwise models; Colley if you want no margin dependency | They use indirect comparisons; can include anchors or synthetic teams to connect groups. |
| Moderate cross-play, some common opponents | Elo/Glicko with strength of schedule adjustments; hybrid models | They gain stability from repeated updates, and connections carry information. |
| Frequent cross-games, lots of data (dense graph) | Any well-tuned system: SRS, Massey, modern Elo, etc. | Data abundance resolves ambiguity; margins & schedule still matter. |

---

## Practical considerations when choosing/implementing

- **Anchor or prior ratings:** If you have teams with no matches, they need a baseline (e.g. last season, average expectations).  
- **Uncertainty representation:** When teams rarely play, rating should have large uncertainty; you might treat them more cautiously (e.g. in predictions).  
- **Schedule connectivity:** Making sure your matchup graph is connected; if not, you might need “phantom” games or synthetic links, or accept that cross-group comparisons are weak.  
- **Margin adjustments & home/away effects:** If you have little data, these often cause more noise than benefit unless carefully modeled.  

---

## Conclusion

If I had to pick one “best” system for handling teams that rarely play each other, **a Bradley–Terry model (or its Bayesian variant)** is the strongest overall: it directly makes probabilistic inferences from indirect comparisons, can incorporate priors for disconnected teams, and offers uncertainty. **Colley Matrix** is a close runner-up especially when you want a simpler, bias-free system focused on win/loss. For dynamic settings, Elo-style models with strength-of-schedule and uncertainty adjustments are also excellent.

If you tell me more about your specific use-case (how many teams, how sparse the schedule, how important margins are, whether you need predictions vs. rankings), I can recommend and possibly help you design one tailored for your needs.
